Preflight

OOP Foundations

Understand the mental model before you code

What You'll Learn

1 Explain OOP and why games use objects and classes
2 Distinguish class vs object, attribute vs method
3 Read a simple UML class diagram and identify public vs private
4 Understand engine vs student code and how validators work

Key Terms

Term Definition
Class A blueprint that defines attributes and methods
Object An instance created from a class blueprint
Attribute Data stored inside an object
Method A function inside a class that operates on object data
Encapsulation Protecting internal data by using methods as the access point
Inheritance Building a new class by reusing and extending a parent class
Polymorphism Same method name, different behavior in different classes
Abstraction Defining what something can do without showing how it does it (often with abstract classes or interfaces)
Composition One class owns another class as a part of itself (has-a)
Aggregation A weaker has-a relationship where objects are shared

Reading UML

- Private or protected
+ Public
-> Returns

Access Modifiers in Python (Concept)

Visibility Python Convention
Public No underscore, open to use anywhere
Protected Single underscore (example: _items). A convention: "use inside the class or subclass."
Private-ish Double underscore (example: __items). Name-mangling discourages outside use.

Python does not enforce access modifiers like Java or C#. It uses naming conventions to support encapsulation. In this project, inventory items are stored in a protected list to encourage safe access through methods.

OOP Principles Map

Principle In This Project
Encapsulation Level C: Inventory uses a protected list; access through methods
Inheritance Level B: Brute and Scout inherit from Player
Overriding Level B: Brute and Scout override a method to describe their specialty
Polymorphism Level B: Same method name, different class behavior
Composition Level C: Player has an Inventory
Aggregation Concept only: one object uses another without owning it
Abstraction Concept only: the engine expects methods to exist, not how they are made

Engine vs Student Code

Engine Runs the game, loads rooms, handles combat, prints maps. You do not edit it.
Student Defines classes and methods in the student folder. The engine calls your code.
Validator Checks that your classes and methods exist and behave correctly before you play.

Level Workflow

  1. Read the worksheet and review the UML diagram
  2. Open the student files and add the required code
  3. Run python3 validate.py to check your work
  4. Run the game to see your code in action
